abstract: A learned cost model that predicts query runtimes is trained on measurements from one machine. When the database moves to other hardware, its plans stay the same but their runtimes change, each by its own factor. We ask how to adapt such a model from $k$ queries measured on the new machine: which queries to run, how to use their runtimes, and how many are enough. On PostgreSQL we timed the same plans of 1,162 TPC-H and TPC-DS queries in six environments: a laptop and a server, each with all its processors or pinned to one, the server also pinned to two, and the laptop also with a small buffer pool. No single factor describes the slowdown between two environments: most of its variance lies between query templates, so a speed factor stops improving after a few queries. A correction that fits separate lines for serial and parallel plans and adds an offset for every measured template brings the moved model, with one measured query per template, to an error (geometric mean over templates of the median Q-error) of 1.10 on TPC-H and 1.19 on TPC-DS, close to the same correction on a model trained on the new machine; fine-tuning a DACE-style neural cost model on the same queries gains at most 2%. On templates never measured, no correction we tried is on average more than 2% better than the speed factor. We then fixed hypotheses and timed new data. On TPC-H at ten times the scale the errors follow these results, but two of five repeated tests miss. On the Join Order Benchmark, whose queries differ widely within a template, the model errs by 2.36 even when retrained on the new machine, no correction gains much, and only the test on new templates holds; boosted trees and a neural model fit these queries better, and correcting the neural model works as well as fine-tuning it. We report every test as registered.

sections.body:
Learned cost models predict runtimes far better when they are trained on the system they predict, but a move to new hardware changes each query's runtime by its own amount. Systems either retrain on the new machine, rescale every prediction by one speed factor, or describe machines with features.

The question is: with k queries run on the new machine, which queries should they be, how should their runtimes be used, and how large must k be? The study times 1,162 queries from 115 templates of TPC-H and TPC-DS in six environments that run identical plans. It then tests its hypotheses on TPC-H at scale factor 10 and on the Join Order Benchmark. Its contributions are a dataset, a comparison of corrections and selection strategies, a negative result for new templates, two rounds of registered tests, and recommendations.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: A runtime model moved to new hardware can be corrected from a few measured queries; this paper asks which, and how many.

sections.body:
The source model predicts the log runtime of a query from its plan features, having been trained on machine A. On machine B, its log error on a query is the log slowdown plus the source model's residual on A:

$$
e(q)=\delta(q)+u_{A}(q)
$$

where $\delta$ is the log slowdown and $u_{A}$ the residual on A. A correction estimates the slowdown from the k measured log errors. The template share measures how much of the slowdown's variance lies between templates, which decides whether one speed factor can describe a move. Accuracy is the Q-error, and a method's error is the geometric mean over templates of the median Q-error of their test queries.
sections.heading: Problem and Background
sections.headline: A query's slowdown on new hardware is its own factor, so corrections need runtimes measured there, and template share measures how much a constant explains.

sections.body:
The primary source model, the forest model, fits a line in log total cost and a random forest to its residuals, using 19 plan features. A neural plan model reimplements the DACE architecture and trains on root runtimes only, with 19,732 parameters on TPC-H.

Corrections act on the k log errors. The speed factor is their mean. The ridge correction is a penalized regression with an unpenalized intercept. The template correction fits a line with separate terms for parallel plans, then adds a mean residual offset for each measured template. Baselines include refitting the forest on the measured queries, a template lookup, and the oracle, which refits on the whole target pool and is a reference rather than a bound. Selection strategies include random, round robin, k-center, D-optimal and plan class.
sections.heading: Methods Compared
sections.headline: Six corrections and six selection strategies are compared against refitting, a neural fine-tune, and an oracle reference.

sections.body:
Six environments run identical saved plans on copies of one database: a laptop and a server, each with all processors or pinned to one processor, a smaller buffer pool on the laptop, and the server pinned to two processors. TPC-H at scale factor 1 has 680 queries from 22 templates, and TPC-DS has 482 queries from 93 templates.

Queries are split inside each template into a pool, from which the k queries are drawn, and a test set. Each query runs in three passes, and a label is the median over passes of the median of three timed runs. The median Q-error between two passes of one query is 1.03 to 1.09 per environment and workload. The protocol draws k from 5 to 200 queries over 20 random orders and scores every correction on the test set.
sections.heading: Experimental Methodology
sections.headline: Identical plans were timed in six environments on TPC-H and TPC-DS, with corrections scored on held-out test queries.

sections.body:
Table II gives seven of the 30 ordered pairs per workload. Over all pairs, 0.69 to 0.94 of the variance of the log slowdown lies between templates, against at most 0.08 (TPC-H) and 0.22 (TPC-DS) between two passes on one machine. Pinning to one processor gives parallel plans a median slowdown of 2.05 to 2.66, while serial plans slow by 0.92 to 1.12, and that one bit explains 0.44 to 0.61 of the variance.

Table III shows that on one processor, operators inside the parallel part of a plan take longer, while serial operators keep their speed. With a small buffer pool, index scans slow by 1.3 to 1.9 times. In the second round, H2 and H3 fail on TPC-H at scale factor 10. On the Join Order Benchmark only H4 holds, and the template share is below 0.5 in the two pairs between the laptop and the server.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: No single factor describes the slowdown: 0.69 to 0.94 of its variance lies between templates.

sections.body:
Measure one query per template, chosen round robin, because on TPC-H and TPC-DS the shift is mostly per template. Avoid the cheapest query of a template, since short queries shift differently. Correct the best model you have rather than refitting it: refitting on the measured queries was far worse up to one query per template on TPC-H and TPC-DS.

Expect the processor count to act through parallel plans: a correction that knows the plan kind lowered the error from 1.41 to 1.28 with ten queries on TPC-H. No correction beat the speed factor by more than 2% on new templates in the first round, and the remaining error is the model's own. On the Join Order Benchmark the forest model erred by 2.36 even when trained on the new machine, and a better source model lowered that error most.
sections.heading: Lessons
sections.headline: Measure one query per template, chosen round robin, and do not expect corrections to help on templates never measured.

sections.body:
Learned runtime models are usually trained for one deployment. Hardware moves have been handled by rerunning a benchmark and retraining (T3), by fine-tuning on a rerun workload (DACE), or by refitting per-operator coefficients from queries run on the new machine (QCFE). Model shift, a fitted line from source to target performance, has been used for configurable software, and it fails for multithreaded programs or severe changes. OneProxy adapts a latency predictor from about 50 measurements using one global factor plus sparse per-operator deviations.

Older calibration work fits cost formulas per machine or per query class, a precursor of the per-template offsets studied here. This paper adds a controlled measurement of how much of a hardware shift a handful of queries can absorb, and of which queries to run.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier work moves cost models with retraining, fine-tuning, model shift or per-template calibration; this paper adds a controlled measurement.

sections.body:
External validity: the study uses one database system and two physical x86 machines, both virtualized. Its SF1 data fit in memory in every environment, and the extension uses data ten times larger but not larger than memory. Queries ran warm and one at a time, and plans are fixed, so a move that also changes settings or plans is out of scope.

Internal validity: pairs of a workload reuse environment labels, so they are not independent replications. The Join Order Benchmark test set holds about one query per template, so its intervals are wide. The server is shared, so its passes started at quiet hours and every pass was checked for level shifts. Construct validity: the neural model reimplements DACE's architecture and trains on root runtimes only, not on DACE's pretrained model.
sections.heading: Threats to Validity
sections.headline: The study covers one database system, two virtualized machines and data that fit in memory.

sections.body:
In all four workloads of both rounds, one measured query per template, with an offset for each template on the moved model, came on average within 3% of the same correction on a model trained on the new machine. Whether the corrected model is accurate depends on the model. On TPC-H at both scales and on TPC-DS it came close to the oracle. On the Join Order Benchmark the forest model erred by more than a factor of two even when trained on the new machine, and boosted trees and a neural model fit that benchmark better.

For templates never measured, no correction was much better than the speed factor. Operator-level corrections, other database systems, plans that change with the machine, and data larger than memory are the next steps.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: In these environments one measured query per template brought the moved model within 3% of the same correction on a retrained model.
